subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Gift Exchange in Labor Markets
description: A micro-lesson that makes Gift Exchange in Labor Markets usable.

hook.text: Henry Ford doubled wages in 1914. Economists called him crazy. Productivity surged and turnover plummeted. He profited.

buildup.text: Akerlof's gift exchange model: paying above market wage is a gift. Workers reciprocate with above-market effort.

discovery.text: Efficiency wages work because workers interpret high pay as respect. They respond with loyalty, not because they must.

twist.text: Monitoring destroys the gift. If you watch workers closely, the wage feels like a transaction, not a gift. Effort drops.

climax.text: Trust and generosity in labor markets create value beyond the contract. Social exchange adds to market exchange.

punchline.text: Pay like you trust them. They will prove you right.

quiz.question: What does Akerlof's gift exchange model predict?
options: Higher wages always lead to inflation
Above-market wages are reciprocated with above-market effort
Workers only respond to strictly enforced contracts

details.summary: Gift exchange theory shows that employers who pay above-market wages receive extra effort from employees in return. Workers reciprocate generosity with loyalty and productivity, creating a positive cycle that pure self-interest models cannot explain.
details.whyItMatters: Gift exchange explains why firms pay above equilibrium wages and why satisfied employees produce more. The relationship between pay fairness and productivity goes beyond incentives to include reciprocity and social obligation.
takeaways: Above-market wages are reciprocated with above-minimum effort
Workers treat fair pay as a gift that creates a social obligation
Gift exchange explains wage rigidity and efficiency wages in labor markets

faq.question: Why would a firm voluntarily pay above market wages?
faq.answer: George Akerlof showed that above-market wages function as gifts that elicit reciprocal effort, loyalty, and lower turnover. The extra productivity and reduced hiring costs offset the higher wage bill, making generosity economically rational.

faq.question: Does gift exchange work in all workplace settings?
faq.answer: It works best when employees can observe the generosity and when effort is somewhat discretionary. In highly monitored settings with rigid output requirements, the reciprocity mechanism is weaker because effort cannot vary much regardless of pay.
